meta.title: AI Call Analysis: feedback on interviews, team syncs and presentations | PairUX
meta.description: Turn on AI call analysis before a PairUX call and get a feedback report afterwards: talk time, speaking pace, filler words, what landed, what to practice, and moments to replay.

callAnalysisPage.eyebrow: AI call analysis · Pro and Team
callAnalysisPage.title: Find out how the call really went.
callAnalysisPage.intro: Turn on AI call analysis before your interview, team sync or presentation. When the call ends you get a private report: a score, what worked, what to fix, the numbers behind it, and the moments worth replaying.

interviews.title: Interviews
interviews.body: Question by question: how each answer landed, where it ran long or stayed vague, and a stronger way to say it. Interviewing someone else? It reviews your questions and how well you listened.

teamSyncs.title: Team syncs
teamSyncs.body: Decisions made, questions left hanging, where the meeting drifted, and every commitment with its owner, so nothing is lost between syncs.

presentations.title: Presentations and demos
presentations.body: Your opening, through-line and close, where the room was likely lost, and what was on screen: slide density, legibility, and whether the screen matched what you said.

callAnalysisPage.measuredBody: The numbers are counted from the transcript, with each speaker told apart, and the written feedback cites them. When the report says you spoke 70% of an interview, it is a fact you can check.

measured.m0: Share of talk time for every speaker
measured.m1: Speaking pace in words per minute
measured.m2: Filler words per 100 words, and which ones

how.s0: Before the call, switch on AI call analysis on the start screen (pairux.com, the desktop app or the mobile app) and pick the kind of call. Recording the call turns on with it, and you can turn that off.
how.s1: During the call, your app uploads the call audio and a still of your shared screen every 20 seconds. Everyone who joins sees that the call is being recorded for analysis.
how.s2: After the call, the audio is transcribed with speakers told apart and an AI coach writes your report. It arrives by email and lives under Call analyses on your dashboard.

privacy.p0: The choice is made before the call starts and cannot be switched on halfway through.
privacy.p1: Every participant sees a notice for the whole call, on the web, desktop and mobile apps.
privacy.p2: Reports and recordings are private to the host, or to the team or organization the call was held in, and can be deleted at any time.
privacy.p3: Keep the recording off and the audio is deleted as soon as the report is written.
privacy.p4: On a phone, only your own microphone is recorded; start from pairux.com or the desktop app to capture everyone.

meta.title: Agentic Pair Programming with moshcode | PairUX
meta.description: Work with a teammate in the same live coding-agent session. Use moshcode for a shared terminal and PairUX to review the screen and app together.

agentic.title: Two people. One agent session.
agentic.intro: Pair programming still needs shared context when an AI agent writes the code. Bring a teammate into your live moshcode session, then use PairUX to review what the agent builds and decide the next step together.

s0.title: Start with one live session
s0.body: Run moshcode on your development machine and open its session at app.moshcode.sh. You and your teammate follow the same agent output and work in the same terminal.

s1.title: Bring your team into the session
s1.body: Create an organization and team in moshcode, add your teammate using their account email, then share the session with that team. Read access lets them watch; writer access lets them send input to the running session.

s2.title: Review the result together in PairUX
s2.body: Share your terminal, editor, or app preview with PairUX. Your teammate joins from a browser to see the work in context. Approve remote control when you want them to use your mouse and keyboard too.

agentic.permissionsNote: moshcode team permissions govern access to the terminal session. PairUX remote control is a separate choice that the screen-sharing host approves. Use either or both, depending on how you want to collaborate.
agentic.contractorTitle: A practical way to onboard a contractor
agentic.contractorP1: Add a contractor to your team and let them watch your first session with read access. Walk through the task, the agent’s output, and the running app. When they are ready to participate, grant writer access so they can work with you in that same session.
agentic.contractorP2: You can also use this workflow to investigate a failing test, compare an agent’s implementation with the intended behavior, or review a change before merging it. Everyone sees the work as it happens.

agenticPairProgramming.title: Agentic pair programming
agenticPairProgramming.description: Work with a teammate in one live coding-agent session. Share the terminal through moshcode and review the screen together in PairUX.
agenticPairProgramming.scenario: You want a teammate to help guide an agent while it works in your development environment.
agenticPairProgramming.outcome: A shared understanding of what the agent changed and what to do next.

s0.title: Start a shared terminal
s0.body: Open your live moshcode session and share it with your team.

s1.title: Bring the app into view
s1.body: Share your editor or app preview through PairUX.

s2.title: Work through the next step
s2.body: Review the result together and decide what to ask the agent next.

aiCodeReview.title: Review AI-generated code
aiCodeReview.description: Walk through the diff, tests, and running app together before an agent’s changes become a merged pull request.
aiCodeReview.scenario: An agent has produced a large change. A reviewer needs to understand its behavior, not just read a summary of the patch.
aiCodeReview.outcome: A reviewed change with clear fixes, follow-up tests, and a shared merge decision.

s0.title: Open the evidence
s0.body: Share your editor with the diff, task requirements, and test output visible. Explain what you asked the agent to change.

s1.title: Try the behavior together
s1.body: Run the app and exercise the important paths. Approve remote control if the reviewer wants to try an edge case directly.

s2.title: Turn findings into the next edit
s2.body: Agree on corrections and ask your coding agent to make them. Review the new diff and rerun the relevant checks before merging.

debuggingWithAgents.title: Get a stuck agent moving
debuggingWithAgents.description: Bring a second person into a failing test or a loop of unsuccessful fixes. Inspect the evidence and choose the next experiment together.
debuggingWithAgents.scenario: Your coding agent keeps changing code without fixing the failure. A teammate can help spot a missing assumption or an environment problem.
debuggingWithAgents.outcome: A reproducible failure and a focused next step for the agent.

s0.title: Show the failure as it happens
s0.body: Share the terminal and reproduce the issue. Walk your teammate through the error, the recent changes, and what has already been tried.

s1.title: Test one explanation
s1.body: Inspect logs, configuration, and the running app together. Grant remote control when your teammate needs to explore the same environment.

s2.title: Give the agent better direction
s2.body: Write down the reproduction steps and the evidence behind your chosen fix. Ask the agent for a focused change, then check the original failure again.

contractorOnboarding.title: Onboard contractors in context
contractorOnboarding.description: Let a new teammate watch a real task, learn your codebase and agent workflow, then participate when they are ready.
contractorOnboarding.scenario: A contractor is joining your project and needs to understand how you use agents, review changes, and decide when work is ready to ship.
contractorOnboarding.outcome: A teammate who understands your workflow and can take on the next task with context.

s0.title: Start with a real task
s0.body: Share your development screen and explain the project, the task, and how you brief your coding agent. Let the contractor observe the first pass.

s1.title: Explain the decisions
s1.body: Walk through the agent’s output, the tests, and the running app. Show where you accept a suggestion and where you ask for another approach.

s2.title: Let them take a turn
s2.body: Approve PairUX remote control for a guided edit. If you also use moshcode, give them writer access to a shared team session when they are ready to send terminal input.

productDesignReview.title: Review the app with product and design
productDesignReview.description: Show the app an agent is building to the people who will judge the result. Try the flow together and turn feedback into specific changes.
productDesignReview.scenario: A working prototype is ready, but the interaction, wording, or layout needs feedback from someone outside the code.
productDesignReview.outcome: Concrete acceptance criteria and an agreed list of changes to the working app.

s0.title: Share the working experience
s0.body: Open the app preview and share that window in PairUX. Walk through the task a real user should be able to complete.

s1.title: Let the reviewer explore
s1.body: Invite feedback as you navigate, or approve remote control so the reviewer can try the flow on your machine.

s2.title: Close the feedback loop
s2.body: Turn observations into specific requests for your coding agent. Show the updated app in the same session and agree on what is ready.

remoteSupport.title: Unblock someone’s AI workflow
remoteSupport.description: Help a teammate configure a tool, understand an error, or recover a broken local workflow while you both see the same screen.
remoteSupport.scenario: An agent or development tool works on one machine but fails on another. Screenshots and copied error messages are missing the context.
remoteSupport.outcome: A working setup and a person who understands how the issue was resolved.

s0.title: Have them show the problem
s0.body: The person with the issue hosts a PairUX session and shares the relevant tool window. Join from your browser and watch them reproduce the failure.

s1.title: Guide the fix in their environment
s1.body: Explain the next check and let them perform it. Request remote control when hands-on help is useful; the host decides whether to approve it.

s2.title: Verify the whole workflow
s2.body: Ask them to run the original task again. Leave them with the steps that fixed the issue so they can recognize it next time.

liveAiWorkshops.title: Teach a live AI coding workshop
liveAiWorkshops.description: Show an audience how you brief an agent, inspect its work, and handle mistakes while building something real.
liveAiWorkshops.scenario: Your team wants to learn an agent workflow by watching the decisions and corrections that a polished demo usually leaves out.
liveAiWorkshops.outcome: An audience that has seen the full path from a task brief to a checked result.

s0.title: Set up a focused demonstration
s0.body: Choose a small task and share the terminal, editor, or app you will use. Pick a PairUX plan that fits your room’s listener capacity.

s1.title: Show the reasoning behind the prompts
s1.body: Explain the context you give the agent and why. Pause at key moments to inspect the diff, run tests, and discuss an unexpected result.

s2.title: Practice reviewing the result
s2.body: Have the group suggest edge cases and follow-up changes. Run those checks in view so participants see how you decide whether the work is ready.

aiNoteTaker.title: AI note taker
aiNoteTaker.description: Turn on AI call analysis before a team sync and leave with the decisions, open questions and action items, plus feedback on how the meeting ran.
aiNoteTaker.scenario: Your team wants to stay focused on the shared work and leave with useful notes for the next session.
aiNoteTaker.outcome: A reviewed recap of the work, the decisions, and the next steps.

s0.title: Turn on AI call analysis before the call
s0.body: On the start screen, switch on AI call analysis and choose "Team sync". Everyone who joins sees that the call is being recorded for analysis.

s1.title: Read the report
s1.body: After the call you get a summary, the decisions reached, the questions left open, and every action item with its owner, next to feedback on how the meeting ran.

s2.title: Carry context into the next task
s2.body: Share the action items with the team, or use the summary to brief a teammate or prepare the next request for your agent.

meta.title: About
meta.description: Learn about PairUX - the open source collaborative screen sharing tool.

about.title: About PairUX
about.subtitle: Building the collaborative tools we wish existed
about.missionP1: PairUX was born from frustration. After Slack acquired Screenhero and shut it down, remote pair programming became unnecessarily difficult. Existing tools either lack remote control, require expensive licenses, or force you into vendor lock-in.
about.missionP2: We believe collaborative screen sharing should be accessible to everyone. That's why PairUX is open source, with transparent pricing and no artificial limitations.
about.buildingBody: PairUX is a desktop application for collaborative screen sharing with simultaneous remote control. Think Screenhero, but modern, open source, and cross-platform.

buildingList.b0: Real-time screen sharing with low latency
buildingList.b1: Multiple participants can control the shared screen simultaneously
buildingList.b3: Works across macOS, Windows, and Linux
buildingList.b4: Viewers can join from any browser

about.openSourceBody: PairUX is released under the MIT license. You can view, modify, and contribute to the code on <link>GitHub</link>. We welcome contributions from the community.
